hook.text: Here are two hundred thousand customers, each with a satisfaction score out of a hundred.

truth.text: Their true average is seventy. But say you can only ask five hundred of them.

question.text: Does it matter WHICH five hundred?

random.text: Pick them at random, and their average comes out at sixty-nine point six. A little low... but close.

easy.text: Now take the five hundred who are easiest to reach. Happy customers answer surveys, so say anyone above seventy-five is eleven times as likely to be picked.

high.text: This sample averages eighty and a half. That's more than ten points too high.

again.text: Was that just bad luck? Draw again... and again, a hundred times each.

both.text: The random averages land on both sides of seventy, about half above and half below.

every.text: The easy ones land near eighty, every single time.

name.text: A miss that always points the same way has a name. It's bias.

bigger.text: So here's the obvious fix. Ask more people. Grow both samples from fifty customers to twenty thousand.

steadier.text: Both get steadier as they grow, and at about the same pace.

closing.text: But only the random one is closing in on seventy.

wrong.text: The easy sample just becomes a sharper and sharper estimate of the WRONG number.

steady.text: At twenty thousand, one customer in ten, it's rock steady... and still almost ten points high.

digest.text: This went wrong for real in nineteen thirty-six. The Literary Digest mailed out ten million ballots for the presidential race.

back.text: Nearly two point four million came back. A huge sample... but the people who chose to reply leaned toward the challenger, Alf Landon.

call.text: So the Digest called it for Landon, with Roosevelt on just forty-three percent.

gallup.text: George Gallup asked far fewer people, chosen to mirror the voters, and put Roosevelt on fifty-six.

result.text: Roosevelt got sixty-two and a half, and won every state but two.

lesson.text: Two point four million answers couldn't fix who was answering.

two.text: So every estimate can miss in two ways.

variance.text: Variance is the scatter from one sample to the next.

bias.text: Bias is where the scatter is centered, and more data leaves it right where it was.

method.text: Only a better method moves the center.
